items.title: Twelve Marks Each of Future, Present, and Past — and Doctrine Three Closes

items.zh: 應知未來有十二種相故。一、因所顯相，二、體未生相，三、待眾緣相，四、已生種類相，五、可生法相，六、不可生法相，七、未生雜染相，八、未生清淨相，九、應可求相，十、不應求相，十一、應觀察相，十二、不應觀察相。
items.en: It should be understood that the future has twelve marks: first, the mark of being made manifest through a cause; second, the mark of a substance not yet arisen; third, the mark of awaiting an assembly of conditions; fourth, the mark of belonging to a kind already arisen elsewhere; fifth, the mark of a phenomenon still capable of arising; sixth, the mark of a phenomenon no longer capable of arising; seventh, the mark of a not-yet-arisen defilement; eighth, the mark of a not-yet-arisen purity; ninth, the mark of what should rightly be sought; tenth, the mark of what should not be sought; eleventh, the mark of what should be contemplated; twelfth, the mark of what should not be contemplated.

items.zh: 當知現在亦有十二種相。一、果所顯相，二、體已生相，三、眾緣會相，四、已生種類相，五、一剎那相，六、不復生法相，七、現雜染相，八、現清淨相，九、可憙樂相，十、不可憙樂相，十一、應觀察相，十二、不應觀察相。
items.en: It should be understood that the present likewise has twelve marks: first, the mark of being made manifest as a result; second, the mark of a substance already arisen; third, the mark of an actual assembly of conditions; fourth, the mark of belonging to a kind already arisen; fifth, the mark of lasting but a single instant; sixth, the mark of not arising again once spent; seventh, the mark of present defilement; eighth, the mark of present purity; ninth, the mark of what is genuinely delightful; tenth, the mark of what is not delightful; eleventh, the mark of what should be contemplated; twelfth, the mark of what should not be contemplated.

items.zh: 當知過去亦有十二種相。一、已度因相，二、已度緣相，三、已度果相，四、體已壞相，五、已滅種類相，六、不復生法相，七、靜息雜染相，八、靜息清淨相，九、應顧戀處相，十、不應顧戀處相，十一、應觀察相，十二、不應觀察相。
items.en: It should be understood that the past likewise has twelve marks: first, the mark of a cause already passed; second, the mark of a condition already passed; third, the mark of a result already passed; fourth, the mark of a substance already destroyed; fifth, the mark of belonging to a kind already ceased; sixth, the mark of never arising again; seventh, the mark of defilement now stilled; eighth, the mark of purity now stilled; ninth, the mark of what should rightly be looked back on with longing; tenth, the mark of what should not be looked back on with longing; eleventh, the mark of what should be contemplated; twelfth, the mark of what should not be contemplated.

items.title: The Fourth Doctrine: A Self That Persists Through the Five Aggregates

items.zh: 計我論者，謂如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論：有我、薩埵、命者、生者、有養育者、數取趣者，如是等諦實常住。謂外道等作如是計。
items.en: The doctrine positing a self: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that there exists a self, a sentient being, a life-possessor, one who is born, one who is nurtured, one who repeatedly takes up a destiny — all such terms naming something truly, permanently existing. It is non-Buddhist teachers and others who hold this position.

items.zh: 問：何故彼外道等起如是見，立如是論？答：由教及理故。教如前說。理者，謂如有一，為性尋思，為性觀察，廣說如前。
items.en: Question: Why do those non-Buddhist teachers and others hold this view and establish this doctrine? Answer: Because of scripture and reasoning. Scripture is as explained before. Reasoning means that someone is a speculator by nature and an examiner by nature, as explained at length before.

items.zh: 由二種因故。一、先不思覺，率爾而得有薩埵覺故；二、先已思覺，得有作故。彼如是思：若無我者，見於五事不應起於五有我覺。
items.en: This arises from two causes. First, without any prior deliberation, the sense of a sentient being spontaneously arises. Second, having first deliberately conceived of a self, one is then able to act. They reason thus: were there no self, upon perceiving any of five things, five corresponding senses of "self" ought never to arise.

items.zh: 一、見色形已，唯應起於色形之覺，不應起於薩埵之覺。二、見順苦樂行已，唯應起於受覺，不應起於勝劣薩埵之覺。三、見已立名者名相應行已，唯應起於想覺，不應起於剎帝利、婆羅門、吠舍、戍陀羅、佛授、德友等、薩埵之覺。
items.en: First: upon seeing a bodily form, one should only ever arrive at the sense of a bodily shape, never at the sense of a sentient being. Second: upon witnessing what accords with pain or with pleasure, one should only ever arrive at a sense of mere feeling, never at a sense of a sentient being as superior or inferior. Third: upon seeing one already given a name and the conduct associated with that name, one should only ever arrive at a sense of mere conception, never at a sense of this sentient being as a warrior, a brahmin, a merchant, a labourer, or as "Buddhadatta" or "Guṇamitra" and the like.

items.zh: 四、見作淨不淨相應行已，唯應起於行覺，不應起於愚者、智者薩埵之覺。五、見於境界，識隨轉已，唯應起於心覺，不應起於我能見等薩埵之覺。由如是先不思覺，於此五事唯起五種薩埵之覺，非諸行覺。是故先不思覺，見已率爾而起，有薩埵覺故，如是決定知有實我。
items.en: Fourth: upon seeing conduct that is either pure or impure, one should only ever arrive at a sense of mere formation, never at a sense of this sentient being as foolish or wise. Fifth: upon seeing consciousness follow along with its object, one should only ever arrive at a sense of mere mind, never at a sense of "I am the one who sees" and the like. Yet since, without prior deliberation, these five things each give rise to a sense of a sentient being rather than a sense of mere formations, and since this sense arises spontaneously the very instant of perceiving, they conclude with certainty that a real self must exist.

items.title: The Second Reason: Self Assumed Wherever Deliberate Action Occurs

items.zh: 又彼如是思：若無我者，不應於諸行中，先起思覺，得有所作。謂我以眼當見諸色，正見諸色，已見諸色，或復起心，我不當見。如是等用，皆由我覺行為先導。如於眼見如是，於耳鼻舌身意、應知亦爾。
items.en: They further reason thus: were there no self, one could not, among the formations, first conceive an intention and thereby come to act. That is: "I shall see these forms with my eye," "I am now seeing these forms," "I have already seen these forms" — or else the thought arises, "I shall not see." All such functions are led by a prior sense of "I." As with seeing through the eye, so too should it be understood with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

items.zh: 又於善業造作、善業止息、不善業造作、不善業止息、如是等事皆由思覺為先方得作用，應不可得。如是等用，唯於諸行，不應道理。由如是思，故說有我。
items.en: Further, the performing of wholesome karma, the ceasing of wholesome karma, the performing of unwholesome karma, and the ceasing of unwholesome karma — such actions, too, could only ever function given a prior deliberate intention; without one, they could never be found to occur at all. Such functioning, they conclude, could never belong to mere impersonal formations alone — this makes no sense. It is by reasoning in this way that they maintain a self exists.

items.title: Four Dilemmas That Dismantle the Sense of a Self

items.zh: 我今問汝，隨汝意答。為即於所見事起薩埵覺？為異於所見事起薩埵覺耶？若即於所見事起薩埵覺者，汝不應言：即於色等計有薩埵、計有我者，是顛倒覺。若異於所見事起薩埵覺者，我有形量，不應道理。或有勝劣，或剎帝利等，或愚或智，或能取彼色等境界，不應道理。
items.en: I now ask you, answer as you see fit: does the sense of a sentient being arise directly within what is seen, or apart from what is seen? If directly within what is seen, then you should not also claim that positing a sentient being, positing a self, directly within form and the rest, is itself a distorted perception. If apart from what is seen, then for the self to have any size or shape makes no sense; for it to be superior or inferior, a warrior or a brahmin, foolish or wise, or capable of apprehending form and the rest as its object, likewise makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？為唯由此法自體起此覺耶？為亦由餘體起此覺耶？若唯由此法自體起此覺者，即於所見起彼我覺，不應說名為顛倒覺。若亦由餘體起此覺者，即一切境界各是一切境界覺因，故不應理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: does this sense arise solely from the aggregates' own substance, or also from some other substance? If solely from the aggregates' own substance, then arriving at a sense of self directly within what is seen should not be called a distorted perception after all. If also from some other substance, then every object whatsoever would equally be the cause of every other sense of self — which makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？於無情數有情覺，於有情數無情覺，於餘有情數餘有情覺，為起為不起耶？若起者，是即無情應是有情，有情應是無情，餘有情應是餘有情，此不應理。若不起者，則非撥現量，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: does a sense of a sentient being ever arise regarding something insentient, a sense of the insentient regarding something sentient, or a sense of one sentient being regarding a different one — or does this never happen? If it does happen, then the insentient would have to actually be sentient, the sentient insentient, and one being actually another — none of which makes sense. If it never happens, then this denies what is plainly observed every day — which likewise makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？此薩埵覺為取現量義？為取比量義耶？若取現量義者，唯色等蘊是現量義，我非現量義，故不應理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: does this sense of a sentient being take its object through direct perception, or through inference? If through direct perception, then only the aggregates — form and the rest — are ever objects of direct perception; a self is never an object of direct perception at all, so this makes no sense.

blocks.text: Today closes the third doctrine with a list of twelve marks for each of the three times, and opens the fourth, the central one for any Buddhist: the doctrine of a **self** (計我論). The refutation of self runs through the next three days and is one of the most thorough in Buddhist literature.
Missing from Ru-Yi's translation (0305b29–c03), now supplied in our own: the formal question why outsiders hold the self-doctrine, answered "through scripture and reasoning".

The treatise gives twelve marks each for future, present, and past. The future includes what has a cause but has not arisen, and what "is no longer capable of arising". Venerable Miào Jìng's example: after an arhat cuts off craving, no future existence in any realm can arise. The present includes what has arisen and not ceased, "lasting but a single instant". His image: whirl a stick of incense and the eye sees a ring of light, though there is only a succession of instants.

He draws a practical use from it. When someone insults you, "the moment the contemplation of impermanence appears, the insulter has already ceased." The one who spoke and the words are already gone; what remains is our holding on.

The past includes what should and should not be looked back on. Master Cháng Bǎi: "With regret lodged in the heart like an arrow, one can't practise. If you did wrong and have repented, repentance purifies; don't dwell on it."

The fourth doctrine says there truly and permanently exists "a self, a sentient being, a life-possessor, one who is born, one who is nurtured, one who repeatedly takes up a destiny". Venerable Miào Jìng notes that 數 in the last name (數取趣, *pudgala*) is read *shuò*, "again and again": the one who takes up result after result. Master Cháng Bǎi: this is held by non-Buddhists "and, within Buddhism, a group called the Vātsīputrīya", who hold a person "neither apart from nor identical to the aggregates".

Venerable Miào Jìng recounts asking Master Yìnshùn why Chinese schools favoured teachings about a buddha-nature that can sound like a self. The answer: "Because they like it." Beings find non-self hard to accept.

subs.head: Two reasons for believing in a self

blocks.text: The doctrine arises from two causes. First, "without any prior deliberation, the sense of a sentient being spontaneously arises": we simply feel there is someone there. Second, "having first deliberately conceived of a self, one is then able to act": action seems to need an agent.
These are the two kinds of self-grasping from Day 22, innate and constructed, now presented as arguments.

subs.head: Four dilemmas against the first reason

blocks.text: Is this spontaneous sense of a being about what is really a being, or not? Both teachers point out that we often mistake: from a distance a burnt tree looks like a person; a motionless sentry looks like a tree. Does the sense grasp its object by perception or by inference? Not by perception, because "only the aggregates are ever objects of direct perception; a self never is". Not by inference, because "even foolish children, incapable of reasoning" have it.
Try it in meditation: look for the self you feel. What you find each time is a feeling, a thought, a sensation, the aggregates. The treatise is describing that search.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, how many marks do the future, present, and past each have?
quiz.why: "The future has twelve marks"; "the present likewise has twelve"; "the past likewise has twelve." Master Cháng Bǎi: this establishes that past and future are unreal and the present real, refuting the doctrine, while giving practitioners a way to regard the three times.

quiz.q: The present's fifth mark is "lasting but a single instant." What image does Venerable Miào Jìng use?
options: whirling a stick of incense, the eye sees a ring of light — really just instant after instant
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Whirl a stick of incense and our eyes see a ring of light." The ring seems continuous but is a succession of instants. He also remarks that the *Śūraṅgama*'s tenfold revealing of seeing "displays permanence," which sits uneasily with contemplating impermanence.

quiz.q: Venerable Miào Jìng says contemplating the present's "single instant" helps counter what in daily life?
options: anger — when someone insults you, with impermanence in view, the one insulting has already ceased
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "You think, 'That person is insulting me' — the moment the contemplation of impermanence appears, the insulter has already ceased." He adds that when people part saying "see you again," they in fact can never see that same moment again — the mark of "not arising again."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what names does the self-doctrine posit as truly and permanently existing?
options: self, sentient being, life-possessor, one born, one nurtured, one who repeatedly takes up a destiny
quiz.why: "There exists a self, a sentient being, a life-possessor, one who is born, one who is nurtured, one who repeatedly takes up a destiny — all such terms naming something truly, permanently existing." Venerable Miào Jìng: this lists six; the *Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom* sixteen, the *Diamond Sūtra* four — the outsiders effectively add a sixth thing, "self," to the five aggregates.

quiz.q: The text says "non-Buddhists and others hold this," rendered "non-Buddhist teachers generally." According to Master Cháng Bǎi, who else does "and others" include?
options: the Vātsīputrīya within Buddhism, who hold a self "neither apart from nor identical to the aggregates"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "These are the non-Buddhists and, within Buddhism, a group called the Vātsīputrīya, who also cling to a self neither apart from nor identical to the aggregates." Translation and reading note mention only non-Buddhists (logged in the correction list). C holds the three-times doctrine.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, from which two causes does the self-doctrine arise?
options: first, a sense of a being arises spontaneously without deliberation; second, deliberate intention precedes action
quiz.why: "First, without any prior deliberation, the sense of a sentient being spontaneously arises. Second, having first deliberately conceived of a self, one is then able to act." Master Cháng Bǎi: seeing someone, one effortlessly thinks "that's Zhang San" — the first; "I want to see, I want to hear" — the second.
